Control of such use will concentrate vehicles and people in areas or on trails, perhaps aggravating the problem of litter and sanitation, but making the solution more easily accomplished.
Signing areas for public information will have a visual impact on users and non-users. Signs must be so designed and located to command the attention of the user and thus may detract from the natural scenery or landscape. This impact can be minimized through utilization of other means of communication such as news media and public meetings. However, adequate posting must be improved to permit enforcement of any restrictions. This will detract from the natural scene, but the location and design of signs can provide minimal conflict with the landscape.
The public lands are reservoirs for a substantial amount of our national and natural heritage, ranging from historical sites to archeological findings. The control of ORV would substantially reduce actual and potential harm for those values for which the Department of the Interior has the charge to administer.
Non-users will still object to interference with their relatively unrestricted use of the public lands and, if they live near a designated area, may object to the noise and inconvenience. They may welcome restrictions, but may resent concentrated ORV use within some areas because it will infringe on their values within that area, as regards noise, exhaust emissions, tracks, trails, etc. However, they may profit by other areas being closed to ORV and thus allow their more leisurely pursuits unimpaired. Conservationists may decry intensified resource use and erosion within established use areas. Bureaus will monitor the activity to ensure adequate controls to protect the environment.
In essence, growth of public interest in ORV use has outstripped easy control of controversial impacts. The current thrust will be to alleviate this controversy by providing space for users and space for non-users and protection of the natural legacies with which several Interior bureaus are charged.
Implementation of the Executive Order and Secretarial memorandum will also impose a substantial impact upon the Department of the Interior. Additional manpower and financial resources will be needed to designate areas, develop facilities, post signs, and particularly to police and enforce ensuing regulations.
